id: Body of Rags, International Bridge Between the US & Mexico

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Is it alive? —neither a head, legs nor arms! ................... ... torpid against the flange of the supporting girder . ? an inhuman shapelessness, knees hugged tight up into the belly Egg-shaped! —William Carlos Williams, 1950 visit to El Paso, from “Desert Music” Yes, I am a body of rags lying here on the bridge waiting for a hot rain to wash me open, dissolve me off the bridge because this border is closed. I rot on the boundary line and can’t enter Juarez, pennies thrown at me when a drunk El Pasoan returns in the darkness and sees my shape that makes him hurry across. No head, decades ago they threw it in the river without my screams. My arms were the first to go when I couldn’t climb the wall. I can never leave this bridge. I live on the pure line that divides countries and grabs my hunger from sliding into Mexico with my outstretched hands. I still have my knees. I used to be sold in Juarez and smuggled into El Paso, the egg that floated down the Rio Grande to break hundreds of miles away before being thrown back. I stay on the bridge and can’t move. Do not cross to El Paso without wiping your shoes of me, one foot on US concrete, the other scraping away at my Mexican rags. When I struggle against the wire fence, I make sure I salute two flags.

Keywords: Egg, William, Carlos

outputs.L1:
> “Is it alive? —neither a head, legs nor arms!  
> ... torpid against the flange of the supporting girder...  
> an inhuman shapelessness, knees hugged tight up into the belly  
> Egg-shaped!”  
> —William Carlos Williams, following his 1950 visit to El Paso, from “Desert Music”

Yes, I am a body of rags lying here on the bridge, waiting for a hot rain to wash me open, to dissolve me from the bridge, because this border is closed. I rot on the boundary line, unable to enter Juarez. Pennies are thrown at me when a drunken El Pasoan returns in the darkness, sees my shape, and hurries across.

No head. Decades ago, they threw it into the river without my screams. My arms were the first to go when I could not climb the wall. I can never leave this bridge. I live on the pure line that divides countries, stretching out my hands to keep my hunger from sliding into Mexico.

I still have my knees.

I used to be sold in Juarez and smuggled into El Paso—the egg that floated down the Rio Grande, only to break hundreds of miles away before being thrown back. I remain on the bridge, unable to move.

Do not cross into El Paso without wiping your shoes of me: one foot on U.S. concrete, the other scraping away at my Mexican rags. When I struggle against the wire fence, I make sure to salute two flags.

outputs.L3:
The speaker imagines themself as a mutilated, rag-covered body trapped on a bridge at the U.S.–Mexico border. Suspended between Juárez and El Paso, they are unable to enter either city and instead remain fixed on the boundary line separating Mexico from the United States. This position makes the bridge more than a physical setting: it becomes a symbol of exclusion, liminality, and the impossibility of belonging fully to either nation.

The body’s missing head and arms evoke the brutal realities of border violence, failed migration, and the bodily consequences of enforcement. Stripped of both identity and agency, the speaker appears reduced to an object that can be moved, traded, or discarded. References to being sold, smuggled, and thrown back across the Rio Grande reinforce this dehumanization, suggesting exploitation by traffickers or institutions and a cycle of repeated displacement. Rather than reaching safety or finding a home, the speaker is continually pushed from one side of the border to the other.

The closing image of saluting both flags captures the speaker’s divided identity. Although they are rejected by both countries, they are still compelled to acknowledge each nation’s authority. The gesture is therefore deeply ironic: without arms, the speaker cannot literally salute, and without acceptance from either side, allegiance becomes forced and hollow. Ultimately, the image presents the border as a place where national identity fractures, leaving the speaker caught between two countries but claimed by neither.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the U.S.–Mexico border not simply as a geographical line but as a site of physical and psychological destruction. At its center is a mutilated, immobilized body stranded between the two countries. The speaker’s damaged condition reflects the violence experienced by migrants and other marginalized people whose lives are shaped by borders. Unable to move freely or claim a secure place on either side, the speaker becomes a disturbing symbol of exclusion, displacement, and political abandonment.

Surreal imagery intensifies this sense of suffering. The body appears fragmented and transformed into part of the border landscape, blurring the distinction between a human being and the territory that confines them. Through personification, the border becomes more than an inanimate boundary: it functions like an active, hostile power capable of trapping, dividing, and dehumanizing people. The speaker’s physical wounds therefore suggest not only individual pain but also the broader damage caused by restrictive immigration systems, racial prejudice, and state violence.

The speaker’s position on the boundary is especially significant. Although physically connected to both the United States and Mexico, the speaker is accepted by neither. This state of suspension represents a divided identity: the speaker exists between national, cultural, and political categories without being permitted to belong fully to any of them. The border creates an impossible condition in which a person can be present in two places yet remain excluded from both. Identity becomes something imposed and fractured rather than freely chosen.

At the same time, the poem refuses to place responsibility entirely on one nation. Because the speaker lies between the two countries, both sides are implicated in the speaker’s suffering. Neither offers rescue, recognition, or genuine belonging. The boundary that supposedly separates the nations instead exposes their shared participation in systems that neglect vulnerable people. In this way, the poem challenges the idea that borders merely provide order or security. It reveals how they can produce instability, erase individuality, and turn human beings into political problems.

Ultimately, the mutilated body embodies the human cost of national division. Its immobility suggests that marginalized people are not only prevented from crossing borders but also denied the ability to determine their own futures. By combining bodily violence, surrealism, and personification, the poem transforms the border into a symbol of social and political cruelty. It argues that when nations define belonging through exclusion, people caught between them are left wounded, voiceless, and without a place they can safely call home.
outputs.L5:
William and Carlos stood in the quiet kitchen, staring at a single **egg** on the table. Neither remembered who had placed it there.

“It could be breakfast,” said William.

“Or the beginning of something,” Carlos replied.

Morning light slipped through the window, turning the shell pale gold. For a moment, the egg seemed to contain every possibility: hunger and nourishment, fragility and life, an ending and a start.

William reached for the frying pan. Carlos reached for a pencil.

In the end, one made breakfast while the other made a poem.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about a mutilated, homeless body trapped on the bridge between El Paso and Juárez, using an excerpt from William Carlos Williams’s “Desert Music” as an epigraph.
counterfactuals.output:
> “Only the poem / only the made poem”  
> —William Carlos Williams, *“Desert Music”*

**PORT OF ENTRY**

At the bridge’s midpoint the body becomes a country no country will admit.

Not *a man*, the papers insist. Not *a woman*. Not *alive enough* for asylum, not *dead enough* for removal. A remainder under emergency foil, silver tongue flickering in exhaust. One leg ends in a bandage the color of border dust. One hand is absent, yet the wrist keeps reaching—toward El Paso’s glass, toward Juárez’s smoke, toward the river translating sewage into light.

Cars inch past. Windows rise.

The body says HOME, but the word has been mutilated too: H—ME, HO—, a door without hinges. Customs asks for identification. The body offers scars, sutures, the blackened moons of old injections. The scanner reads: **NO FIXED ADDRESS.** The scanner reads: **ANOMALY.** Beneath the blanket, ribs count backward.

North: sirens polished clean.

South: factories changing shifts.

Below: the Río Grande, thin as a failed signature.

Someone has tied a supermarket bag around the body’s remaining shoe. Inside the bag: a comb with three teeth, an orange peel, a photograph rubbed faceless, a motel key to a room demolished years ago. Evidence of residence. Evidence of weather. Evidence that once the body stood before a mirror and negotiated with its own reflection.

By noon, sunlight amputates the shadow.

By dusk, the bridge lights stitch it back badly.

The officers change. The traffic changes. The body does not cross. It inhabits the verb between *to leave* and *to arrive*, conjugated by wind: I almost, you almost, we almost. Mouth opening. No sound but coins of breath dropping through the grate.

Night comes wearing two cities.

The body, homeless even inside itself, curls around the invisible house of its pain. Above it, flags practice their separate hungers. Below it, water carries every name without checking documents.

At midnight the bridge dreams it is only a bridge.

At midnight the body dreams it is whole.

Neither dream is permitted entry.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal first-person border poem in which a rag-covered, egg-shaped figure lies on an international bridge, unable to enter either Mexico or the United States.
counterfactuals.output:
**Between Flags**

I lie where the bridge forgets its river,  
an egg wrapped in the rags of old weather,  
my face tucked beneath a century of cloth.

To my left, México opens  
like a red mouth full of marigolds.  
To my right, the United States  
clicks its bright metallic teeth.

Neither country will hatch me.

My papers are feathers.  
My name is written in rain.  
When the guards ask where I was born,  
I point to the crack between lanes,  
where ants carry crumbs  
from one republic to another.

Trucks pass through my sleep.  
Their shadows stamp my body  
with temporary visas.

Below, the river changes languages  
without permission.

I try to crawl north—  
the bridge lengthens.

I turn south—  
the bridge lengthens.

So I remain:  
a soft border inside a hard border,  
an unopened moon in a nest of asphalt,  
rag-covered, breathing,  
claimed by neither flag.

At night, the customs booths close their eyes.  
Stars smuggle themselves overhead.

I listen for the smallest sound—  
not a gun, not a gate,  
but the delicate fracture  
of my shell,

as if I might emerge at last  
into a country with no name,  
carrying nothing  
but the bridge on my back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a politically charged prose poem about migration, violence, and divided identity at the U.S.–Mexico border. Include imagery of missing limbs, the Rio Grande, wire fences, two flags, and shoes scraping away Mexican rags.
counterfactuals.output:
At the border, the Rio Grande carries names no government will pronounce, brown syllables turning in the current like saints refused a church. On one bank, a child counts the missing limbs of history—an uncle’s hand in the desert, a mother’s foot beneath a freight train, a country amputated from itself—and on the other, floodlights bleach every face into evidence. Wire fences stitch the horizon with a surgeon’s cruelty, pretending the wound is a seam.

Above the checkpoint, two flags snap in the same hard wind, each claiming the air, each teaching the body to divide its heart. I belong here, says one half. I survived there, says the other. Between them, rifles translate hunger into threat, and men in uniforms ask blood for its papers.

Morning arrives in polished shoes, scraping away Mexican rags from the courthouse steps, as if poverty were dirt, as if a nation could clean its conscience by grinding cloth into dust. But the rags cling to the soles; the dust enters the lungs. The river keeps crossing without permission. The dead keep crossing in photographs. And the living, carrying two flags inside one rib cage, learn that identity is not a bridge but the body stretched across it—trembling, accused, refusing to break.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Using William Carlos Williams’s description of an “inhuman shapelessness” seen during his 1950 visit to El Paso, imagine that the figure speaks and tells its own story.
counterfactuals.output:
They called me an inhuman shapelessness because the heat would not hold my edges.

It was 1950, and El Paso lay white beneath the sun—rail lines, dust, low roofs, the hard seam of the border. I stood where the city frayed into desert, wrapped in cloth the color of old smoke. The doctor-poet saw me from a passing car. For an instant I entered his eye as a blot, a bundle, a form without a name.

But I had names.

My mother called me Luz because I was born before dawn. My husband called me *mi vida* until the river took his voice. At the laundry they called me señora. At the checkpoint they called me “you there.” The children, when they were hungry, called me Mamá.

That morning I was carrying everything I owned: two dresses, a photograph, a tin cup, three letters tied with blue thread, and a pair of shoes too small for my youngest son. The bundle bent my back and erased my arms. Wind pressed my skirt against my legs, then filled it again, making me now thin, now enormous. Perhaps that is what the poet saw: a body refusing to remain one body.

He saw no face. I had lowered it against the sand.

He saw no hands. They were buried beneath the weight.

He saw no human outline because poverty had redrawn me.

Yet I saw him clearly: pale sleeve at the window, spectacles catching light, his gaze quick with alarm and wonder. He wished to make an image of me. I wished to cross the street before the truck came.

For years afterward, I lived inside his phrase. Inhuman. Shapeless. A darkness at the edge of a bright American road.

So let me give the darkness a mouth.

I was tired. I was forty-three. My left knee ached in cold weather. I could mend a torn shirt so finely the wound disappeared. I knew which cactus fruit could be eaten and which clouds promised no rain. I had laughed until milk came through my nose. I had buried one child and raised three. I feared policemen, fever, and the price of flour. I did not fear the desert, though the desert had tried to unmake me.

No shape? I had the shape of a woman under a burden. The shape of a country divided by a line it could not see. The shape of labor made invisible by those who needed it. The shape of grief wrapped tightly so it would not spill.

And inhuman?

No. What was inhuman was the distance between his window and my feet. The glass. The speed. The glance that turned a life into weather.

Still, I forgive him. He saw that something was there, something his words could not contain. Perhaps shapelessness was not my absence but my escape: I would not become his symbol, his beggar, his border ghost. I flowed beyond the outline he gave me.

Look again.

The car has passed. The dust settles. I lift my head.

I am still walking.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, fragmented monologue narrated by a body abandoned on the El Paso–Juárez bridge, condemned to live on the boundary line and embody the human cost of a closed border.
counterfactuals.output:
They left me where the painted line forgets which country owns the dust.

My left hand in El Paso.

My right hand in Juárez.

My face turned toward the river, though I can no longer see it.

The bridge keeps me.

At noon, heat enters my bones like a second sentence. At night, the floodlights bleach me clean of history. Officers pass. Boots pass. Tires pass. Everyone belongs somewhere for the length of a document.

I belonged to a mother once.

To a room with a blue cup.

To a name spoken through a bad phone connection.

Now they call me *obstruction*.  
Now they call me *incident*.  
Now they argue over jurisdiction.

No one says: body.

No one says: ours.

The line runs beneath my ribs. It has learned my pulse, or what remains of it. North—south. Legal—illegal. Before—after. A thin stripe of paint strong enough to divide a life, too weak to carry its weight.

I hear the gates close again.

Metal answering metal.

On one side, people wait with papers softened by sweat. On the other, people wait with photographs. Between them, I practice being a country no one recognizes.

My mouth is full of unfinished crossings.

A child’s shoe.

A grandmother’s medicine.

A worker’s alarm ringing in an empty room.

The last message: *I’m almost there.*

Almost.

That is the nation they gave me.

The river whispers beneath the bridge, pretending water has no memory. But it remembers ankles. Names. The frantic arithmetic of breath. It remembers how the border moved through us long before we tried to move through it.

Sometimes the wind lifts my sleeve, and both flags tremble.

Not for me.

Never for me.

They built walls to make absence orderly. They sealed the gates and called the silence security. Yet every night I grow heavier with those who cannot cross: the hungry, the hunted, the returning, the ones whose children sleep a mile away under another law.

They enter me.

I become crowded.

I become the closed door’s shadow.

At dawn, officials photograph the line, careful not to photograph my face. By noon, my outline is another map. By evening, the commuters look away with the discipline of the living.

Still, I remain.

Half warning.

Half witness.

Whole wound.

If they move me north, the south will accuse them. If they move me south, the north will deny me. So I am condemned to this exact inch of nowhere, where sovereignty holds its breath and mercy requires authorization.

Listen.

The bridge groans in its sleep.

It knows what it was made for.

Crossing.

Crossing.

Crossing.

And here I lie, the cost of refusing the verb.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
